concept.name: Risk budgeting
concept.definition: A portfolio construction approach that allocates risk rather than capital: each asset, asset class, or strategy is assigned a budget for its contribution to total portfolio risk, and weights are solved so realized risk contributions match those budgets; the special case of equal budgets for all assets is the risk-parity (equal risk contribution) portfolio.
concept.intuition: Instead of deciding '60% of my money in stocks', you decide 'stocks may consume at most 60% of my total risk' - because equal dollars in stocks and bonds produce wildly unequal risk.
concept.mechanics: With risk contribution CRC_i = w_i*(Cw)_i/sigma_p, budgets b_i (summing to 1) are imposed by solving w_i*(Cw)_i = b_i * w'Cw for all i; for equal budgets the ERC solution equalizes all component risk contributions. Risk budgeting became a popular alternative to Markowitz optimization after the 2008 crisis because it needs only covariance estimates, not return forecasts.
concept.formula: Find w such that w_i*(Cw)_i / sigma_p = b_i for all i, with sum_i b_i = 1; ERC is the case b_i = 1/N for all i.
concept.failure_modes: Risk budgets calibrated on historical covariances break in crises when correlations jump; equal-risk portfolios typically need leverage to match the expected return of capital-weighted portfolios, adding financing and margin risk.
concept.misconceptions: Risk parity is not 'equal weights': equal capital weights concentrate risk in the most volatile assets, whereas equal risk contributions deliberately hold less of high-volatility assets.
concept.example: In a stock/bond risk-parity portfolio, because stocks are several times as volatile as bonds, the bond weight must be much larger than the stock weight so that each sleeve contributes 50% of portfolio volatility.

citations.source: Thierry Roncalli, Introduction to Risk Parity and Budgeting
